text.p: Germans can hardly wait for "Tourminator" Jan Ullrich's home-coming on Monday.
Little else matters, not even the prospect of Formula One driver Michael Schumacher winning the German Grand Prix on Sunday.
On the same day, Ullrich is expected to ride to victory on the Champs-Elysees, the first-ever German to win the Tour de France, the world's greatest cycle race.

On Monday, Ullrich and his team mates can expect to be welcomed by a huge crowd in Bonn for a party organised by team sponsor Deutsche Telekom. After parading along one of the city's main avenues, they will attend a reception at the town hall.
The 23-year-old from Rostock has emerged with perfect timing as Germany's newest sports star.

"Boris Becker is on the way out, Michael Stich has had enough and nobody knows what Steffi Graf's knee will be up to," wrote Detlef Vetten in the weekly Die Woche. "There was no one else apart from a couple of footballers with little charisma, the Schumachers and the brave (Formula One driver Heinz-Harald) Frentzen."
Now a new face has emerged in one of the few sports in which Germans have traditional not fared well.
No German has worn the leader's yellow jersey since Klaus Peter Thaler in 1978. Dietrich Thurau led for 15 days in 1977.

Over the past few days, Ullrich's boyish, freckled face has appeared on the front page of almost every German newspaper. Reporters have been busy inventing superlatives, from prince to king and giant to "Tourminator," as popular daily Bild has labelled him.

Newspapers elsewhere have called him a man from another planet, but German papers stress that he is home-grown. His background qualifies him as a true all-German hero, an important point in this recently unified country.

Ullrich learned his trade in the East German sports schools and was 14 when the Berlin Wall collapsed in 1989. Soon after, he moved to Hamburg and now lives in the quiet village of Merdingen, in the Black Forest.

All Germans now know that Ullrich has incredibly long legs, the lungs of a horse and a bright future. Girlfriend Gaby, with whom he fell in love at first sight and who gave him his trademark gold earring, has become a favourite with the local tabloids.
In a country where celebrity comes at a price -- ask Steffi Graf or Boris Becker -- the country's newest sports star might find it hard to maintain a semblance of a private life.
His mother, Marianne, 44, who moved the country when she appeared teary-eyed on television after meeting her son at a stage finish in Colmar, France, near the German border, was aware of the risk.
"I'm so happy for my little boy but at the same time I'm worried that things might never be like they were before," she said.
